newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico unveils rules to combat money laundering.
newsitem.headline: Mexico unveils rules to combat money laundering.

text.p: Mexico took a major step toward combating money laundering on Monday when it published a new set of regulations that financial institutions must follow when dealing with large cash transactions.

The ministry rules, published in the Monday edition of the government's Official Gazette, add teeth to loose rules that have made Mexico a haven for laundering millions in illicit drug profits, U.S. authorities allege.

The rules come against the backdrop of increasing opposition in the U.S. Congress to President Bill Clinton certifying Mexico as an aid-worthy ally in the drug war, and a rash of allegations of corruption in high government circles in Mexico.

Meanwhile, a civil case against former Mexican Deputy Attorney General Mario Ruiz Massieu began in a U.S. federal court in Houston on Monday. It seeks to confiscate some $9 million from a bank account.
U.S. prosecutors allege the money came from bribes paid by drug traffickers. Ruiz Massieu said in court filings the money came from a family fortune made in real estate.
Under the new rules, banks, brokerages and exchange houses will be required to inform the authorities of any transactions deemed either "suspicious" or "relevant."

The ministry defines "suspicious" transactions as those not covered by normal patterns of banking conduct, as stipulated in the current Stock Market Act. "Relevant" transactions are those involving cash or monetary instruments worth an equivalent of $10,000 or more.
The new rules, which take effect on May 2, also envisage stricter identification of clients in financial houses.

Financial houses also will be required to submit for approval by the Finance Ministry any manuals for internal use to enable monitoring of financial transactions in accordance with the new guidelines.
